screens.title: Deploying Your VR Application to a Headset
screens.narratorSegment: Launching your VR app on a physical headset is the final, essential test of your work. In this lesson we’ll walk through the exact steps to prepare a Unity project for standalone headsets such as Meta Quest, and for PC-based VR. You will learn what files are produced — an APK for Android headsets, or a Windows executable for PC VR — and why that distinction matters. We’ll cover the Player Settings values you must set: a unique package name, a compatible minimum A P I level, the IL2CPP scripting backend, and the ARM64 target architecture. You will also see how to enable the Oculus XR provider, install Android SDK and NDK tooling, build an APK, and sideload it with adb. Finally, we’ll describe common errors and how to troubleshoot 'device not found' or driver issues so you can get reliable on-device testing. By the end, you’ll understand not just the sequence of clicks, but the reasons behind each requirement and how they affect performance and compatibility. Think about which headset you’ll deploy first and keep that device’s requirements in mind as we proceed.

screens.title: APK vs Windows executable — choosing the right artifact
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment starts with a simple question: which artifact does your target headset expect? Standalone headsets like Meta Quest run Android, so Unity produces an APK. PC-based headsets run on a Windows host and use a native Windows executable. This is more than a file-name difference. An APK packages bytecode and native libraries for the Android runtime; a Windows executable is compiled for x86_64 hardware and expects a PC runtime like SteamVR or the Oculus PC app. Choosing the correct target affects how you compile scripting backends and which architectures you include. For example, Quest requires ARM64 native code and IL2CPP to get good runtime performance. A Windows build will typically use the usual editor or Mono/IL2CPP choices suitable for desktop. A common misconception is that the same build can run on both without changes. In practice, Player Settings, XR plug-in choices, and external SDKs differ between Android and Windows. Concrete example: if you build an APK but forget to enable ARM64, the Quest will refuse to run the app or crash. Key takeaway: always select the platform that matches your headset and check the Player Settings to match that platform’s expectations.

keyIdea.title: Platform fit

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › APK vs EXE — choosing the right artifact
Comparison
APK — Android (Quest)
  • Packaged for Android runtime, needs IL2CPP and ARM64.
  • Installed via sideloading tools such as adb.
  • Requires XR provider for Android (Oculus).
Windows EXE — PC VR
  • Compiled for x86_64 desktop hardware.
  • Requires PC runtime like SteamVR or Oculus PC app.
  • Simpler build but needs a capable PC to run.
Concrete example
You export two builds: an APK for Quest and a Windows folder for PC. The Quest APK must include ARM64 native libraries; the PC build expects the PC runtime and drivers. Attempting to run the APK on a PC or the EXE on a Quest is not supported and will fail.
Key Takeaway
Select the build platform to match the headset and verify architecture and plug-ins before building.
Common mistake
Not switching Build Settings to the correct platform before building, which causes runtime incompatibilities.

screens.title: Switching to Android and configuring Build Settings
screens.narratorSegment: Switching Unity to the Android platform is the first concrete step in producing an APK. Open File, then Build Settings, and select Android from the platform list. Click Switch Platform and wait for Unity to reimport assets; this step can take a few minutes depending on your project size. After switching, open Edit > Project Settings > Player and choose the Android tab. Important fields include Company Name, Product Name, and the unique Package Name — a reverse-domain style identifier such as com. yourcompany. yourapp. Set the Minimum A P I Level to a value compatible with your Quest, often Android 7.1 (A P I Level 25) or higher. These values tell the Android runtime how to install and run your app and prevent mismatches that would block installation. A common misconception is that package name is cosmetic; in fact it determines installer identity and can block updates if duplicated. Example: if you reuse a package name used by another app, Android will refuse to install your APK over it unless the signatures match. After these settings are in place, confirm XR Plug-in Management has Oculus enabled for Android so the runtime initializes on the headset.

keyIdea.title: Switch & configure
keyIdea.text: Switching platform and setting Player Settings correctly are prerequisite steps before you build an APK.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Switching to Android & Build Settings
Step-by-step
  1. Open File > Build Settings.
  2. Select Android and click Switch Platform.
  3. Open Edit > Project Settings > Player > Android tab.
  4. Set Company, Product, and unique Package Name.
  5. Set Minimum API Level ≥ 25 for Quest compatibility.
Example Package Name
Use reverse domain notation such as com.yourname.myfirstvr so Android uniquely identifies your app. This matters for updates and installation.
Why Minimum API matters
Setting it too low can allow incompatible system calls; too high will exclude older devices. Choose the lowest level that supports required XR features.
Misconception
Package name is not just cosmetic; it identifies the app to the OS and affects installation and updates.

screens.title: IL2CPP and ARM64 — scripting backend and architecture
screens.narratorSegment: IL2CPP and ARM64 are two linked configuration choices that determine how your Unity code becomes a native application on Quest. IL2CPP converts your managed C# code into C++ ahead of time, and then the C++ is compiled to a native binary that runs without a just-in-time compiler. This native code generally runs faster and is more predictable on constrained mobile-class hardware. ARM64 specifies the C P U architecture target that the binary is compiled for; modern Meta Quest devices use 64-bit ARM processors, so building for ARM64 ensures the app can run and take advantage of the device’s instruction set. A common mistake is leaving the scripting backend on Mono or not checking ARM64; the result can be a failed build, an app that won’t install, or poor runtime performance. Concrete example: switching to IL2CPP and enabling ARM64 resolves many crash-on-launch issues caused by incompatible native libraries. Key takeaway: IL2CPP + ARM64 are essential for stable, high-performance builds on standalone Android VR headsets. IL2CPP and ARM64 — scripting backend and architecture means il2cpp produces native code and arm64 matches the headset cpu, together ensuring stability and performance on quest.. In practical terms, why il2cpp and arm64 are required for modern quest builds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › IL2CPP & ARM64
Definitions
IL2CPP: A scripting backend that converts managed code into native C++ binaries for ahead-of-time compilation.
ARM64: The 64-bit ARM CPU architecture used by modern standalone headsets like Quest.
Concrete example
If your app crashes on launch, enabling IL2CPP and ARM64 in Player Settings often fixes native library mismatches and improves frame consistency.
Practical checks
  • Open Player Settings > Other Settings > Scripting Backend and select IL2CPP.
  • Under Target Architectures, check ARM64.
  • Rebuild after changing these settings to ensure native libraries are recompiled.
Common mistake
Leaving Mono as the scripting backend or not including ARM64 will likely prevent the Quest from running the app or cause runtime crashes.

screens.title: XR Plug-in Management and External Tools
screens.narratorSegment: XR Plug-in Management connects Unity to the VR runtime the headset expects. After switching to Android, open the XR Plug-in Management settings and enable the Oculus provider for Android so Unity initializes the correct runtime on the device. If you are targeting PC, enable OpenXR or Oculus for the PC Standalone tab. Another crucial check is Unity’s External Tools preferences: confirm the Android SDK, NDK, and Java SDK are installed and correctly pointed to in Edit > Preferences > External Tools. Unity can install these components for you, or you can point Unity to existing installations. If these tools are missing, Unity cannot compile native Android libraries or produce an APK. Example: build failures that mention missing NDK or gradle occur when External Tools are not configured. Common misconception: the XR plug-in alone is sufficient; in reality, missing SDK/NDK tooling will stop builds before they start. Always verify both the XR provider and External Tools before building. XR Plug-in Management and External Tools means enable the appropriate xr provider and configure android sdk/ndk so unity can compile and package a working apk.. In practical terms, enable oculus for android and configure android sdk/ndk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › XR Plug-in Management & External Tools
Enable XR Provider
Open Project Settings > XR Plug-in Management. Under Android, check Oculus. For PC, use OpenXR or Oculus under the Standalone tab.
Why this matters
XR providers register platform-specific runtime entry points and render loops required by the headset.
Configure SDK / NDK
Open Edit > Preferences > External Tools. Ensure paths to Android SDK, NDK, and Java are set, or allow Unity to install them.
Build failure symptom
Errors about missing NDK or gradle indicate External Tools are not configured correctly.
Quick checklist
XR provider enabled
SDK/NDK present
Rebuild after changes

screens.title: Building the APK in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: After configuring Player Settings and confirming the XR provider and external tools, build the APK. Go to File, Build Settings, verify Android is selected, and click Build. Unity will prompt for a folder and filename; choose a clear path such as a dedicated build folder and a filename like MyFirstVR. apk so you can find it for installation. During the build Unity will compile managed code via IL2CPP into C++ and then invoke the Android toolchain to produce an APK. Build times vary depending on project size and whether the NDK needs to be used. A useful example workflow is to keep a MyVRBuild folder and increment filenames with version numbers. If the build fails with messages about missing SDK/NDK or architecture mismatches, return to External Tools and the Player Settings to confirm IL2CPP and ARM64 are enabled. After a successful build you will have a single APK file that can be installed on a Quest using adb. Keep in mind that a signed build is needed for publishing, but for testing a debug-signed APK is sufficient. Building the APK in Unity means use clear build folders and filenames, and check for toolchain errors during the build process before attempting to install.. In practical terms, file > build settings → build — choosing location and filename. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Building the APK
Build steps
  1. File > Build Settings > Android selected.
  2. Click Build and choose folder and filename, e.g., MyVRBuild/MyFirstVR.apk.
  3. Wait for Unity to compile and package the APK.
Tip
Use incremental filenames for quick rollback, and keep a dedicated build folder for each project.
Build output (example)
Building Player: MyFirstVR.apk
Compiling scripts with IL2CPP...
Running Android Gradle build...
Signing APK...
Build succeeded: MyVRBuild/MyFirstVR.apk
If build fails
Check External Tools for SDK/NDK paths, verify IL2CPP and ARM64, then rebuild.

screens.title: Using adb to sideload onto Meta Quest
screens.narratorSegment: Sideloading an APK uses the Android Debug Bridge, or adb. First, enable Developer Mode on your Quest via the mobile app and connect the headset to your PC by USB. In a terminal, run adb devices to confirm the device is recognized; you should see an ID listed as 'device'. If the headset prompts inside its display to allow USB debugging, accept that permission. Once recognized, install the APK with adb install path/to/your/app. apk. The terminal will show progress and report Success when the install completes. If you don’t have a headset, simulate the same terminal commands to learn the workflow: echo commands that mimic the adb output help you practice. A common misconception is that any USB cable will work; the cable must be data-capable, not charge-only. If adb reports an error, try restarting the adb server with adb kill-server and adb start-server, and check drivers on Windows. Concrete example: installing MyFirstVR. apk might display 'Performing Streamed Install' and then 'Success'. Key takeaway: adb is the simple, repeatable bridge between your build artifact and the headset for rapid iteration.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Using adb to sideload
Terminal commands (example)
adb devices
# returns list of connected devices
adb install C:\Users\You\Desktop\MyVRBuild\MyFirstVR.apk
# returns Performing Streamed Install → Success
Simulated flow (no headset)
Run echo commands to mimic adb output so you can practice command order and interpretation.
Connection checklist
  • Enable Developer Mode via the Meta app.
  • Use a data-capable USB cable and ensure the headset shows the USB debugging prompt.
  • Accept debugging and verify with adb devices.
Note
If the device is listed as offline or not found, try restarting the adb server or checking drivers on your PC.

screens.title: Developer Mode and USB debugging
screens.narratorSegment: Developer Mode is a headset setting that unlocks advanced features such as sideloading and USB debugging. To enable it for a Meta Quest, use the Meta Quest mobile app tied to your account and turn on Developer Mode for the device. This permits the headset to accept adb connections from your development machine. When you first connect the headset to your PC, a prompt typically appears inside the device asking you to accept USB debugging from that computer. You must accept this prompt to allow adb to communicate with the headset. A common troubleshooting step is to revoke USB debugging authorizations in the headset settings and reconnect, which forces the prompt to reappear. Example: if you connect and adb devices shows no devices, check Developer Mode is enabled, accept the prompt, and confirm the cable supports data transfer. Many developers assume pairing via Bluetooth is sufficient; it isn’t. USB debugging specifically authorizes low-level adb commands required for installation and logging. Key takeaway: enable Developer Mode and accept the headset prompt to allow adb to function reliably. Developer Mode and USB debugging means developer mode and the headset's usb debugging prompt must be accepted to allow adb to install and log apps.. In practical terms, enable quest-level settings so adb can connect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Troubleshooting common deployment issues
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment issues often fall into a small set of repeatable causes. The most frequent 'device not found' error is caused by a missing or incorrect USB driver, a charge-only cable, or the headset’s USB debugging prompt not being accepted. Troubleshoot by verifying the cable supports data, checking Windows Device Manager for unknown devices, and restarting the adb server with adb kill-server then adb start-server. Another common class of errors is incorrect Player Settings: wrong Package Name, wrong scripting backend, or missing ARM64 will cause install failures or crashes on Quest. A missing Android SDK/NDK produces build-time errors mentioning gradle or ndk; fix this by configuring External Tools and allowing Unity to install missing components. For runtime debugging, Unity Logcat or Debug. Log on the device reveal errors that don’t show in the editor. Example: a build that installs but crashes on launch may log an exception about an unsupported native library — indicating an architecture mismatch. Key takeaway: follow a checklist — cable, USB prompt, drivers, adb server, Player Settings, SDK/NDK, and device logs — to isolate the issue quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
Launching your VR app on a physical headset is the final, essential test of your work. In this lesson we’ll walk through the exact steps to prepare a Unity project for standalone headsets such as Meta Quest, and for PC-based VR. You will learn what files are produced — an APK for Android headsets, or a Windows executable for PC VR — and why that distinction matters. We’ll cover the Player Settings values you must set: a unique package name, a compatible minimum A P I level, the IL2CPP scripting backend, and the ARM64 target architecture. You will also see how to enable the Oculus XR provider, install Android SDK and NDK tooling, build an APK, and sideload it with adb. Finally, we’ll describe common errors and how to troubleshoot 'device not found' or driver issues so you can get reliable on-device testing. By the end, you’ll understand not just the sequence of clicks, but the reasons behind each requirement and how they affect performance and compatibility. Think about which headset you’ll deploy first and keep that device’s requirements in mind as we proceed.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to prepare a Unity project for a specific VR headset, select and verify critical Player Settings for Android builds, use adb to sideload an APK onto a Meta Quest device, and perform basic PC VR builds. Each skill matters for a different part of deployment: correct Player Settings ensure compatibility and performance, adb enables testing on physical hardware, and understanding PC deployment simplifies testing across wired headsets. For example, setting a unique package name prevents installation conflicts, and choosing IL2CPP with ARM64 produces a native binary optimized for Quest performance. You’ll also learn to verify that XR plug-ins like Oculus or OpenXR are enabled so the runtime can initialize correctly on the device. Finally, you’ll practice troubleshooting steps such as accepting the USB debugging prompt and restarting the adb server. Together these objectives let you move from project to headset with confidence and stop common errors before they block testing.

This lab-focused objective set prepares you to carry out a full build and sideload cycle. You will switch the Unity platform to Android, configure the Player Settings for a Quest-compatible build, and run a real or simulated adb workflow. Practically, that means creating a uniquely named package, choosing a minimum A P I level compatible with Quest, enabling IL2CPP and ARM64, and confirming the Oculus XR provider is active. You will build an APK, then either connect a Quest headset and install it with adb install or simulate the adb commands in a terminal if hardware is unavailable. The lab also trains you to use Unity’s Logcat or Debug. Log statements to observe runtime messages and performance indicators while testing. By practicing these steps, you reduce friction during future iterations and make on-device testing routine rather than an occasional, risky step.

Deployment starts with a simple question: which artifact does your target headset expect? Standalone headsets like Meta Quest run Android, so Unity produces an APK. PC-based headsets run on a Windows host and use a native Windows executable. This is more than a file-name difference. An APK packages bytecode and native libraries for the Android runtime; a Windows executable is compiled for x86_64 hardware and expects a PC runtime like SteamVR or the Oculus PC app. Choosing the correct target affects how you compile scripting backends and which architectures you include. For example, Quest requires ARM64 native code and IL2CPP to get good runtime performance. A Windows build will typically use the usual editor or Mono/IL2CPP choices suitable for desktop. A common misconception is that the same build can run on both without changes. In practice, Player Settings, XR plug-in choices, and external SDKs differ between Android and Windows. Concrete example: if you build an APK but forget to enable ARM64, the Quest will refuse to run the app or crash. Key takeaway: always select the platform that matches your headset and check the Player Settings to match that platform’s expectations.

Switching Unity to the Android platform is the first concrete step in producing an APK. Open File, then Build Settings, and select Android from the platform list. Click Switch Platform and wait for Unity to reimport assets; this step can take a few minutes depending on your project size. After switching, open Edit > Project Settings > Player and choose the Android tab. Important fields include Company Name, Product Name, and the unique Package Name — a reverse-domain style identifier such as com. yourcompany. yourapp. Set the Minimum A P I Level to a value compatible with your Quest, often Android 7.1 (A P I Level 25) or higher. These values tell the Android runtime how to install and run your app and prevent mismatches that would block installation. A common misconception is that package name is cosmetic; in fact it determines installer identity and can block updates if duplicated. Example: if you reuse a package name used by another app, Android will refuse to install your APK over it unless the signatures match. After these settings are in place, confirm XR Plug-in Management has Oculus enabled for Android so the runtime initializes on the headset.

IL2CPP and ARM64 are two linked configuration choices that determine how your Unity code becomes a native application on Quest. IL2CPP converts your managed C# code into C++ ahead of time, and then the C++ is compiled to a native binary that runs without a just-in-time compiler. This native code generally runs faster and is more predictable on constrained mobile-class hardware. ARM64 specifies the C P U architecture target that the binary is compiled for; modern Meta Quest devices use 64-bit ARM processors, so building for ARM64 ensures the app can run and take advantage of the device’s instruction set. A common mistake is leaving the scripting backend on Mono or not checking ARM64; the result can be a failed build, an app that won’t install, or poor runtime performance. Concrete example: switching to IL2CPP and enabling ARM64 resolves many crash-on-launch issues caused by incompatible native libraries. Key takeaway: IL2CPP + ARM64 are essential for stable, high-performance builds on standalone Android VR headsets. IL2CPP and ARM64 — scripting backend and architecture means il2cpp produces native code and arm64 matches the headset cpu, together ensuring stability and performance on quest.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

XR Plug-in Management connects Unity to the VR runtime the headset expects. After switching to Android, open the XR Plug-in Management settings and enable the Oculus provider for Android so Unity initializes the correct runtime on the device. If you are targeting PC, enable OpenXR or Oculus for the PC Standalone tab. Another crucial check is Unity’s External Tools preferences: confirm the Android SDK, NDK, and Java SDK are installed and correctly pointed to in Edit > Preferences > External Tools. Unity can install these components for you, or you can point Unity to existing installations. If these tools are missing, Unity cannot compile native Android libraries or produce an APK. Example: build failures that mention missing NDK or gradle occur when External Tools are not configured. Common misconception: the XR plug-in alone is sufficient; in reality, missing SDK/NDK tooling will stop builds before they start. Always verify both the XR provider and External Tools before building. After configuring Player Settings and confirming the XR provider and external tools, build the APK. Go to File, Build Settings, verify Android is selected, and click Build. Unity will prompt for a folder and filename; choose a clear path such as a dedicated build folder and a filename like MyFirstVR. apk so you can find it for installation. During the build Unity will compile managed code via IL2CPP into C++ and then invoke the Android toolchain to produce an APK. Build times vary depending on project size and whether the NDK needs to be used. A useful example workflow is to keep a MyVRBuild folder and increment filenames with version numbers. If the build fails with messages about missing SDK/NDK or architecture mismatches, return to External Tools and the Player Settings to confirm IL2CPP and ARM64 are enabled. After a successful build you will have a single APK file that can be installed on a Quest using adb. Sideloading an APK uses the Android Debug Bridge, or adb. First, enable Developer Mode on your Quest via the mobile app and connect the headset to your PC by USB. In a terminal, run adb devices to confirm the device is recognized; you should see an ID listed as 'device'. If the headset prompts inside its display to allow USB debugging, accept that permission. Once recognized, install the APK with adb install path/to/your/app. apk. The terminal will show progress and report Success when the install completes. A common misconception is that any USB cable will work; the cable must be data-capable, not charge-only. If adb reports an error, try restarting the adb server with adb kill-server and adb start-server, and check drivers on Windows.
